Puzzle 15 · 16 of 16

One canvas on iOS

On iOS, your Compose screen doesn't become UIKit buttons and labels. It's drawn. Here's what UIKit sees, and why VoiceOver and native controls need a bridge.

  • Puzzle 4: An iOS app in one puzzle

    iOS apps are written in Swift, in Xcode, Apple's IDE. Screens are built with UIKit, Apple's screen framework (or the newer SwiftUI). A view controller manages one screen's UI elements and reacts to the user, much like an Activity or Fragment. Swift looks like Kotlin: let is val, var is var, and a class can subclass UIViewController the way yours subclasses Activity.

    Review puzzle 4

  • Puzzle 14: What Compose actually shares

    Compose Multiplatform shares the Compose compiler and runtime with Jetpack Compose, and the same APIs. On Android your build uses Google's Jetpack Compose artifacts; on iOS, desktop and web it uses JetBrains' builds of the same libraries. What's written per target is the platform layer: window, touches, drawing surface, text input and accessibility.

    Review puzzle 14

The problem

Puzzle 14 said the platform layer is rewritten per target. On iOS, does your Column with a Button turn into a UIStackView with a UIButton? If it doesn't, how does VoiceOver know there's a button to read out?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

It doesn't turn into UIKit buttons and labels. Your Swift code hosts the whole Compose screen as one view controller, returned by ComposeUIViewController { App() }. Inside it, Compose draws every pixel itself with Skia, a graphics library for shapes and text, which Kotlin reaches through Skiko ("Skia for Kotlin").

So UIKit sees one view. It doesn't know there's a button at the top or a list below. That has two consequences.

First, accessibility. VoiceOver reads iOS's accessibility tree: the list of on-screen elements with their labels and roles. Compose already knows what each element is, from the semantics that Material components attach, so Compose Multiplatform maps that data into native accessibility objects. A Material Button arrives in the tree as a button. A shape you drew yourself, with no semantics, is invisible to VoiceOver, unless you give it some, for example with Modifier.semantics { contentDescription = "Pay" }, or make it clickable.

Second, native controls. A map, a web view or a video player is a UIKit view that Skia can't draw. UIKitView puts a real one into your Compose layout, and Compose sizes and positions it like any other composable.

And Compose doesn't have to own the whole app: a UIKit or SwiftUI app can show Compose for just one screen, one view controller among its own.

The analogy

A painted mural instead of a shop window full of real objects. Passers-by see the same scene, but a blind visitor needs a guide who knows what each painted thing is (the accessibility tree), and anything that must really open, like a door, is a real door set into the wall (UIKitView).

Check yourself

Your Compose screen on iOS has a Column with a Button. What does UIKit see?

Right. One view, drawn by Compose.

Not quite. UIKit still runs the app; Compose lives inside one of its screens.

Not quite. Compose doesn't create UIKit objects for composables; it draws them itself.

You draw a custom icon button yourself, as plain shapes with no semantics. What does VoiceOver read?

Not quite. UIKit sees one view; what's in the tree comes from Compose's semantics.

Right. No semantics, nothing to read.

Not quite. Skia only draws pixels; it doesn't tell iOS what they mean.

What's the difference between ComposeUIViewController and UIKitView?

Not quite. UIKitView goes the other way: a native view inside Compose.

Right. Opposite directions.

Not quite. That's the two swapped.

Sources
  • Skiko README ("Skiko (short for Skia for Kotlin) is the graphical library exposing significant part of Skia library APIs to Kotlin, along with the gluing code for rendering context"; supported platforms include "Kotlin/Native on iOS")
  • Kotlin docs: Support for iOS accessibility features ("semantics data produced by Compose APIs is now mapped to native objects and properties that are consumed by iOS Accessibility Services. For most interfaces built with Material widgets, this should happen automatically.")
  • Kotlin docs: Integration with the UIKit framework ("To use UIKit elements inside Compose Multiplatform, add the UIKit elements that you want to use to a UIKitView")

What you now know

On iOS, Compose Multiplatform draws your whole UI itself with Skia, through Skiko, inside one hosted view: ComposeUIViewController. UIKit sees one view, not your buttons. So Compose maps its own semantics into iOS's accessibility tree for VoiceOver, and a native control such as a map goes in through UIKitView.
